title: Vector endpoint latency decomposition and kernel handoff for tail reduction
creator: Jordan Rivera
description: Objective: Reduce p95/p99 latency for the Vector (embeddings) API by attacking the end-to-end tail through systematic decomposition, a lightweight kernel handoff for short sequences, and a runtime microbatch controller that avoids stragglers. This ticket coordinates profiling, prototype kernel path, and rollout gating for production traffic.
motivation: Customers with real-time search and semantics use-cases observe high tail latency under mixed load. We need an engineering approach that targets short-sequence fast-paths without regressing throughput or model correctness for long sequences. This aligns with Redwood's thesis around predictable inference economics and reliability.
acceptance_criteria: p99 for 16-token synthetic benchmark reduces by >= 30% compared to baseline across three runs
No decrease >1% in cosine-similarity quality on the dev prompt set (semantic QA eval)
Prototype kernel handoff path passes CI and can be enabled via runtime feature flag
Runtime microbatch controller does not increase average cost/unit by >5% in 72h soak
Gated rollout plan with automated rollback on latency regressions in production
attack_plan: 1) Latency decomposition: add lightweight instrumentation to split E2E request time into queueing, serialization, kernel execution, and KV/cache lookup (2d)
2) Short-seq kernel handoff: implement fast-path that bypasses heavyweight compilation heuristics for requests with seq_len <= 32 (5d prototype)
3) Microbatch controller: implement SLO-aware coalescer that dynamically adapts microbatch target using exponential moving average of queue latency (3d)
4) Speculative prewarm: for high-frequency tenants, prewarm KV cache entries and instantiate fast-path contexts (2d)
5) Profiling & load tests: run mixed-load scenarios (small+long sequences) at 1.5x target QPS to validate no regression (2d)
6) Rollout: feature-flagged canary -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated p95/p99/LR monitors (2d)
7) Post-mortem & tuning: capture p50/p95/p99 deltas, adjust handoff thresholds and hysteresis (ongoing)
progress_updates: 2026-02-26: Added detailed timing spans in the vector service (queue, serialize, kernel_invoke, kv_lookup, postproc). Initial traces show queueing as dominant contributor during bursts.
2026-02-28: Prototype short-seq handoff implemented in runtime: bypasses slow kernel selection and uses sticky precompiled kernels for seq<=32. Unit tests added.
2026-03-03: Microbatch controller v0.1 merged to feature branch. Controller uses EMA(0.2) of queue latency to adjust target microbatch size between 4 and 32.

2026-03-07: Perf run (mixed load): baseline p99=420ms for 16-token workload; prototype reduces to ~220ms on 8-GPU dedicated pool (synthetic replay). Observed 3% throughput drop for heavy long-sequence tails.
2026-03-10: Decision made to increase handoff seq threshold to 48 for customers with >80% short requests after stakeholder review (PM + runtime lead). Preparing canary gating rules.
decisions: Use sequence-length-first heuristic for handoff instead of RTT-only to avoid oscillation under variable RPC latency
Implement hysteresis window of 10s for microbatch controller to reduce thrashing during transient spikes
Feature-flag the fast-path per-tenant with a tenant-level override so enterprise customers can opt-in for maximum predictability
tradeoffs_and_risks: Fast-path increases code-path divergence; risk of maintenance burden and subtle correctness bugs for model-specific kernels
Slight throughput reduction for long-sequence-heavy workloads due to preallocated fast-path resources; mitigated by dynamic fallback to compiler-driven path
Speculative prewarm increases memory usage and may slightly increase cost for low-volume tenants; limited by cap and eviction policy
metrics_expected: Target: p99 down >=30% on short-seq benchmarks (16 tokens)
Target: p95 down >=20% overall for mixed load
Quality: <=1% change in cosine-similarity on semantic dev set
Cost: no >5% increase in token-cost-equivalent for steady-state workloads
